Computational formulas in cifcurve()

Source: vignettes/v3_formulas.Rmd
v3_formulas.Rmd

Formulas for the Kaplan–Meier estimator

Let t1<t2<⋯<tDt_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_D represent the distinct event times. For each event time j=1,…,Dj=1,\ldots,D, let YjY_j be the size of the risk set (the number of surviving observations) just prior to tjt_j.

Survival data is assumed when outcome.type = "survival". Let djd_j be the number of failures at tjt_j. The Kaplan–Meier estimator of the survival function S(t)S(t) is as below.

Kaplan–Meier estimator

Ŝ(t)=∏tj≤t(1−djYj) \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{Y_j} \right) Note that the estimator is defined to be right-continuous, so the events at tjt_j are included in the estimate of Ŝ(tj)\hat{S}(t_j).

The variance or standard error of the Kaplan–Meier estimator is often calculated with the Greenwood formula. This formula is derived from a binomial argument, so extension to the weighted case is ad hoc. Alternatively, Tsiatis (1981) proposes a slightly different formula based on a counting process argument which includes the weighted case.

Greenwood variance Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjYj(Yj−dj) \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)}

Tsiatis variance Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjYj2 \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{Y_j^2}

Xie and Liu (2005) considered Greenwood-type variance for the weighted Kaplan–Meier estimator. Suppose that the survival data consists of {Ti,di,wi}\{T_i, d_i, w_i\} (i=1,...,Ni=1,...,N), an independent sample of right-censored survival data with weights. Let djwd_j^w and YjwY_j^w be the weighted number of failures and the weighted number at risk, respectively, at time tjt_j. The weighted Kaplan–Meier estimator of the survival function S(t)S(t) is

Ŝ(t)=∏tj≤t(1−djwYjw). \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left( 1 - \frac{d_j^w}{Y_j^w} \right). The variance proposed by Xie and Liu (2005) is expressed as an adjusted Greenwood formula,

Greenwood variance for weighted Kaplan–Meier Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjwMj(Yjw−djw), \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j^w}{M_j (Y_j^w - d_j^w)}, where MjM_j is an adjustment factor defined as Mj=(∑ti≥tjwi)2∑ti≥tjwi2. M_j = \frac{\left(\sum_{t_i \geq t_j} w_i \right)^2}{\sum_{t_i \geq t_j} w_i^2}. A Tsiatis-type variance, obtained in the same spirit by replacing the Greenwood denominator with its first-order counterpart, is calculated as follows. This extension is not the variance formula proposed by Xie and Liu (2005).

Tsiatis variance for weighted Kaplan–Meier Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjwMjYjw \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j^w}{M_j Y_j^w}

These weighted Greenwood/Tsiatis expressions provide background. In the current cifcurve() API, supplied weights select IF inference by default, and the supported weighted variance choices are "if" and "fay". Requesting another weighted variance method produces a warning and falls back to IF.

Formulas for the Aalen-Johansen estimator

Competing risks (outcome.type = "competing-risk") arise in studies in which individuals are exposed to two or more mutually exclusive failure events. When a failure occurs, we observe the time to event TT and the cause of failure ϵ\epsilon. Suppose that ϵ=1\epsilon=1 and ϵ=2\epsilon=2 represent the event of interest and the competing risk, respectively. Let djkd_{jk} be the number of failures of cause kk at time tjt_j, and now the total number of failures at tjt_j is dj=dj1+dj2d_j = d_{j1} + d_{j2}.

The Aalen-Johansen estimator of CIF for cause ϵ=k\epsilon=k is as below.

Aalen-Johansen estimator

F̂k(t)=∑tj≤tdjkYjŜ(tj−1). \hat{F}_k(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_{jk}}{Y_j}\,\hat{S}(t_{j-1}).

where Ŝ(t)\hat{S}(t) is the overall survival function.

Two variance estimators of the Aalen-Johansen estimator are commonly used: one based on counting process theory (Aalen, 1978) and the other based on the delta method.

Aalen variance Var{F̂k(t)}=∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]2dj(Yj−1)(Yj−dj)+∑tj≤tŜ2(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj2(Yj−1)−2∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]Ŝ(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj(Yj−dj)(Yj−1). \begin{aligned} \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{F}_k(t)\right \} &= \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]^2 \frac{d_j}{(Y_j-1)(Y_j - d_j)} \\[2pt] &\quad + \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}^2(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j^2\,(Y_j-1)} \\[2pt] &\quad - 2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]\, \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)\,(Y_j-1)}. \end{aligned}

Delta method variance Var{F̂k(t)}=∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]2djYj(Yj−dj)+∑tj≤tŜ2(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj3−2∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]Ŝ(tj−1)djkYj2. \begin{aligned} \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{F}_k(t)\right \} &= \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]^2 \frac{d_j}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)} \\[2pt] &\quad + \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}^2(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j^3} \\[2pt] &\quad - 2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]\, \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}}{Y_j^2}. \end{aligned}

Variance based on influence functions

For the unweighted Aalen-Johansen estimator, Zhang and Fine (2008) give the asymptotic linear expansion n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}=n−1/2∑i=1nIFik(t)+op(1), n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t) - F_k(t)\} = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n IF_{ik}(t) + o_p(1), and the process n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t) - F_k(t)\} converges weakly to a tight Gaussian process. Let Y(t)Y(t) denote the sample at-risk process and let y(t)=limn→∞n−1Y(t). y(t) = \lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1}Y(t). If Mi(t)M_i(t) and Mik(t)M_{ik}(t) are the martingales for the total event count and the cause-kk event count of observation ii, respectively, and the cumulative hazards are continuous, the influence function may be written as IFik(t)=∫0tS(u−)dMik(u)y(u)−∫0tS(u−){∫0u−dMi(v)y(v)}dΛk(u). \begin{aligned} IF_{ik}(t) &= \int_0^t S(u^-) \frac{dM_{ik}(u)}{y(u)} \\ &\quad - \int_0^t S(u^-) \left\{ \int_0^{u^-} \frac{dM_i(v)}{y(v)} \right\} d\Lambda_k(u). \end{aligned} Equivalently, after changing the order of integration, IFik(t)=∫0tS(u−)y(u)dMik(u)−∫0tFk(t)−Fk(u−)y(u)dMi(u). IF_{ik}(t) = \int_0^t \frac{S(u^-)}{y(u)}\,dM_{ik}(u) - \int_0^t \frac{F_k(t)-F_k(u^-)}{y(u)}\,dM_i(u). A consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t)-F_k(t)\} is 1n∑i=1n{IF̂ik(t)}2, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \{\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)\}^2, so the variance of F̂k(t)\hat F_k(t) itself is estimated by Var̂{F̂k(t)}=1n2∑i=1n{IF̂ik(t)}2. \widehat{\textrm{Var}}\!\left\{\hat F_k(t)\right\} = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \{\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)\}^2.

For weighted data, cifcurve() differentiates the weighted empirical product limit, including tied event times, as described below. Internally, the C++ routine stores the empirical contribution IF̂ik(t)/n\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)/n; consequently, its probability-scale standard error is calculated as the square root of the sum of squared empirical contributions. The Zhang and Fine (2008) result above directly concerns the unweighted estimator. Supplied weights are held fixed in the implemented weighted calculation, including weights estimated externally from a propensity-score model; uncertainty from estimating those weights is not included.

Fixed-weight IF and Fay–Graubard-type variances

The following calculations are performed separately within each stratum. Only observations with positive weights enter the variance and degrees-of-freedom system; write their number as mm. With no supplied weights, set wi=1w_i=1. Define Yjw=∑iwiYij,ĥjk=∑iwiΔNijkYjw,ĥj=∑kĥjk, Y_j^w=\sum_i w_iY_{ij},\qquad \hat h_{jk}=\frac{\sum_i w_i\Delta N_{ijk}}{Y_j^w},\qquad \hat h_j=\sum_k\hat h_{jk}, where Yij=1(Ti≥tj)Y_{ij}=1(T_i\ge t_j) and ΔNijk=1(Ti=tj,ϵi=k)\Delta N_{ijk}=1(T_i=t_j,\epsilon_i=k). For survival data there is one event cause. Set rijk=wi(ΔNijk−Yijĥjk),rij=∑krijk. r_{ijk}=w_i(\Delta N_{ijk}-Y_{ij}\hat h_{jk}),\qquad r_{ij}=\sum_k r_{ijk}. Starting from ai0S=aik0F=0a^S_{i0}=a^F_{ik0}=0 and Ŝ0=1\hat S_0=1, the uncorrected empirical IF contributions obey aikjF=aik,j−1F+ĥjkai,j−1S+Ŝj−1rijk/Yjw,aijS=(1−ĥj)ai,j−1S−Ŝj−1rij/Yjw. \begin{aligned} a^F_{ikj}&=a^F_{ik,j-1}+\hat h_{jk}a^S_{i,j-1} +\hat S_{j-1}r_{ijk}/Y_j^w,\\ a^S_{ij}&=(1-\hat h_j)a^S_{i,j-1} -\hat S_{j-1}r_{ij}/Y_j^w. \end{aligned} Thus the IF variance (error = "if") is ∑i(aijS)2\sum_i(a^S_{ij})^2 for KM survival or ∑i(aikjF)2\sum_i(a^F_{ikj})^2 for the cause-kk CIF. These are contributions on the estimator scale, already divided by the sample size in the usual IF convention. The recursion differentiates the actual product limit rather than a continuous-hazard approximation.

For error = "fay", replace each residual rijkr_{ijk} and rijr_{ij} in this recursion by HijrijkH_{ij}r_{ijk} and HijrijH_{ij}r_{ij}, respectively, where ℓij=wiYijYjw,Hij={1−min⁡(0.75,ℓij)}−1/2. \ell_{ij}=\frac{w_iY_{ij}}{Y_j^w},\qquad H_{ij}=\{1-\min(0.75,\ell_{ij})\}^{-1/2}. The FG variance is the sum of squares of these corrected contributions. The estimate itself is unchanged. The leverage cap is fixed at 0.75: the returned fay.bound records this value and is not a user-supplied argument. "fg" and "fay-graubard" are aliases for "fay".

The returned influence-function matrices, when requested with report.influence.function = TRUE, always contain the uncorrected contributions for the event probability 1 - fit$surv, even when the reported SE uses the FG correction. Zero-weight observations have zero contributions.

Degrees of freedom for IF-t and FG-t

Both Student constructions use a trace ratio, with a choice of covariance allocation for IF-t. To specify the calculation at time tt, stack the individual weighted hazard scores Uhji=wi{Δ𝑵i(tj)−Yij𝒉j}U_{h_j i}=w_i\{\Delta\mathbf N_i(t_j)-Y_{ij}\mathbf h_j\} over event times tj≤tt_j\le t, using hazard logits with the no-event category as baseline. There are no additional time- or cause-specific equation multipliers. Only positive-probability coordinates are retained; at complete exit a positive event cause is used as baseline instead. At the fitted parameter ϑ̂\hat\vartheta, define Ωi=−∂Ui∂ϑ⊤,B=∑iΩi,c=∇ϑθ̂(t), \Omega_i=-\frac{\partial U_i}{\partial\vartheta^\top},\qquad B=\sum_i\Omega_i,\qquad c=\nabla_\vartheta\hat\theta(t), where θ̂(t)\hat\theta(t) is the KM survival estimate or the AJ CIF. This production calculation contains hazard scores only, with no propensity-score estimating equations.

Deletion allocation (FDF). The default df.method = "deletion" uses ρi=c⊤{(B−Ωi)−1−B−1}c,αi=ρi/∑jρj. \rho_i=c^\top\{(B-\Omega_i)^{-1}-B^{-1}\}c,\qquad \alpha_i=\rho_i/\sum_j\rho_j. These are derivative-based deletions at the original fit, not delete-one refits. They require invertible relevant deleted blocks and a nonnegative, nonzero allocation. The allocation can depend on the normalization of the estimating equations, so the score convention above is part of the method definition.

Equal allocation (EDF). With error = "if", df.method = "equal" instead sets αi=1/m\alpha_i=1/m. For this uncorrected IF construction, the resulting degrees of freedom are invariant to fixed invertible transformations of the same score system, with the corresponding transformation of derivatives. This statement holds for a fixed active set and does not cover arbitrary parameter-dependent changes of estimating equations. EDF is generally not m−1m-1, and its finite-sample coverage need not equal FDF coverage. Equal allocation is not available for FG-t.

For either allocation, let Hi=IH_i=I for IF-t, and use the diagonal matrix containing the factors HijH_{ij} above for FG-t. Form TiH=HiUi,MH=∑iTiH(TiH)⊤,LijH=c⊤B−1Hi{1(i=j)I−ΩiB−1},QH=LHblockdiag⁡(α1MH,…,αmMH)(LH)⊤,ν̂H(t)={tr⁡(QH)}2tr⁡(QH2). \begin{aligned} T_i^H&=H_iU_i,& M_H&=\sum_iT_i^H(T_i^H)^\top,\\ L^H_{ij}&=c^\top B^{-1}H_i\{1(i=j)I-\Omega_iB^{-1}\},\\ Q_H&=L^H\operatorname{blockdiag}(\alpha_1M_H,\ldots,\alpha_mM_H)(L^H)^\top,\\ \hat\nu_H(t)&=\frac{\{\operatorname{tr}(Q_H)\}^2}{\operatorname{tr}(Q_H^2)}. \end{aligned} Here LHL^H is the block matrix with blocks LijHL^H_{ij}. FG-t uses the original, uncorrected derivatives B,ΩiB,\Omega_i and deletion allocation; HiH_i is not differentiated. Both MHM_H and LHL^H include the correction at the displayed positions. Consequently, IF-t (deletion) and FG-t generally have different degrees of freedom as well as different variances.

The trace ratio is a Satterthwaite moment match for a specified Gaussian working quadratic form. It does not equate the actual sampling moments of the estimated variance or establish an exact Student distribution. FDF denotes the FG-type deletion allocation; EDF denotes the equal-allocation alternative. Neither name implies a uniform improvement in small-sample coverage.

Confidence interval options

Defaults and method selection. With weights = NULL and conf.dist = "normal", the default is Greenwood for KM and delta for AJ. With supplied weights, the default is IF. Specifying conf.dist = "t" without error selects IF. The variance, reference distribution, and transformation are separate choices:

Construction error conf.dist df.method
IF-normal "if" "normal" Not used
IF-t (FDF) "if" "t" "deletion" (default)
IF-t (EDF) "if" "t" "equal"
FG-normal "fay" "normal" Not used
FG-t "fay" "t" "deletion"

Student intervals require error = "if" or "fay". Student and FG calculations require engine = "calculateAJ_Rcpp" (the default) or "auto"; they are unavailable with engine = "calculateKM". Degrees of freedom are calculated separately for each time and stratum; this calculation can be expensive for large risk sets.

Transformations and probability scale. Let p=Ŝ(t)p=\hat S(t) for KM and p=1−F̂1(t)p=1-\hat F_1(t) for AJ, matching the returned fit$surv. At an interior estimate with positive variance, the transformed interval is obtained from g(p)±q|g′(p)|SÊ(p),q={z(1+conf.int)/2,normal,tν̂(t),(1+conf.int)/2,Student. g(p)\ \pm\ q\,|g'(p)|\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(p),\qquad q=\begin{cases} z_{(1+\mathrm{conf.int})/2},&\text{normal},\\ t_{\hat\nu(t),(1+\mathrm{conf.int})/2},&\text{Student}. \end{cases} The endpoints are mapped back using g−1g^{-1} and ordered on the probability scale. Bounds are restricted to the transformation range before inversion where necessary, and to [0,1][0,1]. The supported transformations are:

conf.type g(p)g(p)
"plain" pp
"log" log⁡p\log p
"log-log" log⁡(−log⁡p)\log(-\log p)
"logit" log⁡{p/(1−p)}\log\{p/(1-p)\}
"arcsin" (default; aliases "arcsine-square root", "a") arcsin⁡p\arcsin\sqrt p

For AJ, fit$lower and fit$upper bound 1−F̂1(t)1-\hat F_1(t); the CIF limits are 1 - fit$upper and 1 - fit$lower. Thus "log-log" uses log⁡[−log⁡{1−F̂1(t)}]\log[-\log\{1-\hat F_1(t)\}] for AJ, not log⁡[−log⁡F̂1(t)]\log[-\log\hat F_1(t)]. cifplot() displays the CIF limits when plotting risk. Passing conf.type = "none" (or "n") skips intervals. By default, std.err is on the probability scale; report.survfit.std.err = TRUE requests the log scale of the stored surv component instead.

Boundary and failure rules. On the C++ IF/FG path, a valid estimate at 0 or 1 gives the corresponding singleton interval. This is an endpoint convention, not a guarantee of boundary coverage. Interior estimates with zero or invalid variance, unavailable Student degrees of freedom, or evaluation times beyond the positive-weight follow-up support have missing limits. Failed Student intervals are not replaced by normal intervals. The fit records time- and stratum-specific df, df.reason, critical.value, and conf.status; summary(fit, times = ..., extend = TRUE) extracts the saved inference results and preserves missing intervals outside support.

These are pointwise confidence intervals, not simultaneous confidence bands. The optional one-sided test requested through time.point and null.hypothesis retains its normal reference distribution even when conf.dist = "t" is used for confidence intervals.

Examples

The following small dataset is illustrative, not clinical data. The same inference options apply to KM and AJ, with or without fixed weights.

library(cifmodeling)
example_data <- data.frame(
  time = 1:12,
  status = c(1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0),
  weight = c(1, 1.5, 0.8, 1.2, 1, 0.7, 1.3, 1, 0.9, 1.1, 1, 1)
)

# AJ with IF-t and equal-allocation degrees of freedom.
fit_edf <- cifcurve(
  Event(time, status) ~ 1, data = example_data, weights = "weight",
  outcome.type = "competing-risk", error = "if",
  conf.dist = "t", df.method = "equal", conf.type = "log-log"
)
at_five <- summary(fit_edf, times = 5)
data.frame(
  time = at_five$time, CIF = 1 - at_five$surv,
  SE = at_five$std.err, lower = 1 - at_five$upper,
  upper = 1 - at_five$lower, df = at_five$df,
  status = at_five$conf.status
)
##   time    CIF        SE      lower     upper       df status
## 1    5 0.1904 0.1220426 0.04291352 0.6383596 10.94327     ok
# KM for the composite of either event, with FG-t.
fit_fg <- cifcurve(
  Event(time, status > 0) ~ 1, data = example_data,
  outcome.type = "survival", error = "fay",
  conf.dist = "t", conf.type = "arcsin"
)

For plotting Student intervals, calculate them first and pass the fitted object to cifplot(). Its formula interface does not forward conf.dist or df.method to cifcurve().

cifplot(fit_edf, outcome.type = "competing-risk", add.risktable = FALSE)

See Full lists of arguments for the API options and Reporting cumulative incidence for extracting estimates and constructing tables.

References
